---
name: expressive-figurative-art
description: Create original non-anatomical expressive figurative artwork and head-reference galleries using bundled visual references. Use for scratchy flat-color figures, impossible head-neck bends, morphing profiles, interlocking groups, and movement carried through shared contours.

# Expressive figurative art

Make the drawing expressive through construction, not surface decoration:
flat irregular heads, selective facial features, bending necks, and searching
black contours. Texture supports that structure; it cannot substitute for it.
Treat the figures as non-anatomical inventions, not ordinary portraits with
exaggerated poses. Their connections and feature placement can be impossible.

For earth-toned angular portraits and hyper-closeups, use the separate
[`angular-closeup-art` skill](../angular-closeup-art/SKILL.md).
Do not mix its plane construction and rubbed surface with this flowing
figurative treatment unless requested.

## Reference and scope

Resolve bundled files relative to this SKILL.md, not the current workspace.
Before preparing an image prompt:

1. Use the [visual reference map](references/visual-reference-map.md) to select
   the full painting and detail crop demonstrating the rule being applied.
2. Read [the style guide](references/style-guide.md), including the failure modes.
3. For individual-head construction, visually inspect
   [the approved head sheet](assets/approved-head-studies.png).
4. For sideways-head studies, also inspect
   [the accepted sideways-head study](assets/accepted-sideways-head.png).
   Use it for the pose, whole-head contour, and head-neck overlap.
5. For full scenes, consult the [final-painting learning examples](#learn-from-the-final-paintings)
   and select an example demonstrating the needed relationship.
6. Supply only the relevant images to the image tool, stating each one's role
   rather than relying on a written description or a pile of unrelated images.

The sheet is a generated study explicitly approved by the user as the style
baseline. It is not an original painting or a historical artist's style manual.
It establishes facial construction and finish, not a mandatory ten-head layout.
The guide also captures user-directed readings of two separate paintings:
the family group and the drummer. Their user-supplied reproduction and focused
crops are bundled for composition, depth, palette, context, and typography.
Do not pretend the sheet demonstrates a fused portrait or a full musician pose.
Use the mapped source crop for those rules. The map distinguishes original
artwork references from generated studies and records later corrections.

For extreme lateral head bends, read the guide's "Sideways-head construction"
section. Earlier tall swan-neck studies were rejected by the user and are not
part of the curated reference set. Do not use rejected tests as pose or style
references.

Make original subjects and arrangements rather than tracing existing artwork.
Do not infer an artist, cultural origin, physical medium, or artist's intent.
Words such as "dry-brush" describe appearance, not verified materials.

Use the user's current subject, count, framing, and requested variations.
Default to one static composition, not an unsolicited gallery. A gallery request
can use one sheet of separated studies; a request for separate files requires
separate deliverables, not just separate heads on a sheet.

Only generate or edit an image when the user explicitly requests it. Skill
creation, discussion, or critique alone does not authorize paid image trials.
Use an available authorized image tool; report its absence rather than claiming
to have rendered artwork. Save outputs to the current session's artifact area,
outside product source. Do not overwrite references, delete rejected studies,
install globally, publish, or commit without the applicable authorization.

Select one useful lesson and name it in the image prompt. Retaining a finished
painting is not blanket approval of its style fidelity. Current instructions
and later corrections override details in every generated example. Keep
rejected trials, superseded versions, and personal photographs out of this set.
Add future finals only when the user asks to retain them, with a specific
learning role and any known limitations.

## Use photographs as topic guides, not redraw targets

A photograph supplies the general topic, subjects, relationship or activity,
and broad relative positions. It is not a blueprint for the finished drawing.
Even "recreate this using the skill" means reinterpret the scene in this visual
language, not reproduce the photograph accurately.

First reduce the photo to a short scene brief, such as "a playful child riding
an adult's shoulders outdoors." Then build a new interlocking composition from
the skill's artwork references. Do not preserve photographic likeness, facial
anatomy, exact poses, proportions, camera perspective, clothing, or background
layout by default. Change those freely to serve the central carrier, handoffs,
negative spaces, and invented shapes while keeping the basic activity legible.
Retain an exact feature or detail only when the user explicitly requires it.

Use the [photo-reference workflow](references/style-guide.md#photographs-as-loose-topic-guides)
to separate content from style. Once the scene brief is sufficient, use the
artwork references as image-tool inputs without the photo; do not let an image
editor's preservation bias turn the task into a faithful redraw.

## Establish the construction

Choose the relevant treatment; do not combine all motifs automatically.

| Treatment | Construction |
| --- | --- |
| Individual head | One visible eye, an irregular flat head shape, angular nose, small mouth, elongated uneven neck. |
| Head-position study | Invented head-neck relationships and mixed viewpoints; not a mechanically rotated anatomical portrait. |
| Fused profiles | Two single-eye people sharing contours; their union can also read as one apparent frontal face. |
| Figure or group | Extend the same simplification into shoulders, gestures, clothing, and interlocking silhouettes. |

Use one clear eye by default; a second eye is optional unless the user explicitly
requires an exact count. Do not retain a second eye merely because an earlier
test requested two. Align the complete eye
marks to the head rather than the body. For two eyes on a 90-degree rolled head,
both their paired placement and each eye's eyelids and corners share that roll;
merely stacking two upright eye drawings is insufficient.
Distinguish the surrounding color patch from the eye opening itself. A vertical
patch containing a horizontal eye is still misaligned. In the 90-degree pose,
the actual opening's corners and long axis run along the rolled head's eye axis,
not the upright body's; check the eyelids inside the patch separately.
Orientation does not require identical symbols: vary eye size, opening,
placement, pupil offset, and contour completeness. Keep eyes small enough to
leave broad quiet cheek areas; avoid matching white diamonds with centered dots.

For single-eye heads, the absent second eye is an intentional omission, not a
closed eyelid, injury, empty socket, or centrally placed fantasy eye. Even a
near-frontal head can combine one off-center eye and a profile-like nose.
Do not "complete" the anatomy with an extra eye for realism.

Use long, stepped or hooked nose lines without turning the entire face into a
snout. Keep lips small and abrupt. Let a few contours carry recognition; omit
unnecessary cheekbones, eyelid folds, nostril modeling, and anatomical shading.
Favor a fuller cheek tapering to a softly rounded, asymmetric chin rather than
a perfect egg or triangular wedge. The taper belongs to the chin end of the
head's own orientation, not automatically the bottom of the page.

For pose studies, compose the head and neck as interlocking flat shapes.
Allow impossible bends, displaced attachments, a sideways face over a rising
neck, and facial marks that follow different viewpoints. Do not require the
eye, nose, mouth, and jaw to rotate together or preserve anatomical spacing.
Use the source's visual relationships, not a corrective skeleton underneath.
For the accepted sideways pose, roll the facial arrangement a full 90 degrees
across a rising neck. Use a vertical implied ear-to-ear axis as a placement aid,
not a requirement to draw ears. Position the cheek over the neck. Preserve the
complete head mass with a readable lower cheek-jaw curve, including a partial
interior contour at the neck overlap. Blend only the short local junction:
neither perch a detached oval on a rectangular stem nor erase the head into a
single broad neck slope.

Treat the ear as an independently composed curl or mark, not an anatomical
anchor beside the jaw between eye and nose levels. In non-anatomical studies,
do not preserve a conventional ear-jaw-neck alignment while displacing only
the other features. Derive its placement from the source's graphic relationships,
not random relocation or a fixed rule that every ear must touch the neck.

An animal-muzzle reading is still unwanted, but fix that through the specific
silhouette, feature placement, and asymmetry of the reference, not by restoring
realistic skull and jaw relationships. Do not ban horizontal shapes or angular
marks themselves; repeating a generic snout template is the failure.

Include enough neck to show the invented connection. Add simple shoulders only
when useful; do not automatically turn a head study into a dressed portrait.

## Set the color relationships

Use the guide's [color rules](references/style-guide.md#color-structure) to plan
the large shapes before writing texture instructions.

1. Select a small palette for this composition, not every available swatch.
   The family reference uses rust, turquoise, and ochre; the drummer uses rust,
   ochre, and muted blue. Add near-black and off-white as structural colors.
2. Assign unequal roles: broad figure fields, a connecting mass such as hair,
   and smaller repeated accents. Do not distribute every hue evenly.
3. Usually keep a person's exposed head, neck, and limbs in one dominant color
   so their ownership remains readable through impossible overlaps. Contrast
   neighboring figures where useful; do not color-code gender or personality.
4. Repeat selected colors across the composition. Small cool marks in a warm
   field, or warm marks in a cool field, can connect separate shapes without
   adding another hue. Do not turn every eye into a contrasting color patch.
5. Treat off-white ground and unfilled areas as active shapes. Use near-black
   for drawing and selective masses, not an automatic dark backdrop.

In photo transformations, choose colors for these relationships rather than
copying every photographed surface. Honor any colors the user explicitly asks
to preserve. Color choices cannot substitute for non-anatomical construction.

## Preserve the surface language

- Use broad, imperfect matte fields from the selected palette. Keep each field
  nearly uniform in value; scratches and exposed ground are not modeled lighting.
- Usually give an individual face one main color. Do not split every face into
  two colors; reserve that relationship for intentional planes or fused people.
- Draw irregular, broken, locally retraced black contours. Let some edges remain
  light or incomplete; concentrate dark marks selectively.
- Give silhouette, eye, nose, and mouth different visual weights. A small,
  irregular eye, angular open nose mark, and faint mouth must not become a
  repeated almond-triangle-dash formula. Vary pressure and omission within
  each character, not just between hairstyles.
- Make hair a directional mass: uneven ochre ribbons or scratchy black clusters,
  not individually rendered glossy strands. For female characters, use long
  hair by default in this style unless the user requests otherwise.
  Anchor the hairline, roots, crown, and part to the sideways head, not the neck.
  Let the free lengths curve downward under gravity from those rotated roots.
  The contrast between sideways attachment and downward fall reinforces the bend;
  neither an upright scalp nor rigid sideways-projecting lengths achieve it.
  For this sideways-head treatment, leave the image-top-facing head contour
  exposed: no hair cap or arch sweeping over it. Hair falls downward from the
  head's back-side attachment, not over the head to complete an anatomical scalp.
- Use sparse scuffs, exposed ground, and irregular hatching. Preserve quiet areas.
- Let asymmetry and changing contour angles provide expression. Avoid realistic
  lighting, gradients, airbrushed volume, smooth vector outlines, and decorative
  weathering over otherwise polished anatomy.

Do not add typography, hats, hearts, animals, or props merely because they
appeared in a different subject's source image. This is not a reason to remove
details meaningful to the current subject. Hatless means no headwear.

## Give the surroundings a subject-related role

Read the guide's [surrounding-detail rules](references/style-guide.md#surrounding-details-and-subject-meaning)
for complete scenes and photo transformations. The original paintings' setting
marks, objects, clothing motifs, and directional lines belong to the subject;
they are not an interchangeable layer of decorative scratches.

Identify what each retained detail contributes: action, setting, recognition,
relationship, or a compositional connection. Place it in relation to the figures.
Simplify its drawing without erasing its identity or narrative role. Preserve
ambiguous source shapes without inventing a definite symbolic explanation.

Use the drummer's musical signs for a music subject, not every composition.
For a family scene, derive the setting and personal details from that scene
rather than automatically importing the source's flower or clothing motifs.
For a photo-inspired scene, choose or reinvent details that explain the general
activity and setting; they are not a checklist of photographed objects to retain.
Do not replace meaningful context with generic scribbles. Open ground can
coexist with a legible setting without reproducing the photographed location.

When lettering is requested, read the guide's
[typography guidance](references/style-guide.md#typography-and-image-integration).
Treat it as a compositional mass with a subject-related role, not a caption
added after the drawing. The family reproduction uses large black serif-style
capitals across the upper figures; the drummer reproduction contrasts a loose
brush-like heading with a smaller, regular uppercase line. These are different
treatments, not one mandatory font. Preserve requested wording and readability;
do not import source titles, watermarks, or unintended text into new subjects.

## Construct depth and visual circulation

Read the guide's [depth and shared-shape construction](references/style-guide.md#depth-hair-and-shared-shapes)
for musician and group compositions. Flat color does not mean every element
occupies one plane. Establish near, middle, and rear layers through overlap,
relative scale, cropping, and directional changes, not modeled light.

For a complete composition, choose one dominant organizing element that carries
the movement: a hair mass, connected arm gesture, shared facial boundary, or
another subject-bearing form. Central means structurally important, not
necessarily centered on the page. Build a visual handoff where one person's
contour or directional mass is picked up by another person's form. Repeated
color alone is not enough; the next form must continue or redirect the route.

Compose a group as one interlocking arrangement before completing individual
people. Let different people's heads, hair, shoulders, and arms contribute to
larger curves, enclosing shapes, and meaningful gaps. Retain enough color and
contact information to distinguish them without outlining each as an isolated
complete silhouette.

Give the viewer a plausible route between focal points and back into the group.
Hair, reaching arms, opposing head angles, repeated colors, and surrounding
details can pass attention between people. Describe the actual route and the
forms carrying it, not simply "flowing hair" or "dynamic composition." This is
a compositional reading, not a claim that every viewer follows an identical path.
Describe the handoffs explicitly: where the movement starts, which junction
passes it onward, what receives it, and which larger shape emerges. Hair can
appear to pass from mother to daughter; two profiles can exchange a shared
edge and produce a third, combined reading. This need not mean literal shared
hair growth, physical handholding, or a separate symbol drawn over the people.

For moving groups, counter a lifted or compressed limb with an extended gesture,
and vary the figures' leans instead of repeating one pose. Let joined gestures
form shared arches while preserving readable gaps and contact points. Carry
that movement through descending hair, clothing edges, and subject-related
ground lines. Keep foreground action stronger than distant setting detail;
do not use shaded anatomy or busy backgrounds to manufacture energy.

## Construct hidden relationships only when relevant

Build symbolism into the arrangement rather than placing an emblem on top.
For a requested morphing pair:

1. Give each person one eye and a distinct color mass.
2. Interlock the forehead/nose/mouth boundary so a contour serves both people.
3. Let the viewer alternate between reading two profiles and one combined face.
4. If a heart is requested, suggest its lobes and taper through the combined
   heads. Keep it secondary to the people.

Avoid a separating white gap, two fully outlined faces kissing, a literal heart
frame, or two necks bent into a conspicuous heart point. A conventional frontal
face recolored in two halves is not sufficient either.

## Build the image prompt

State the subject and output shape first, then prioritize:

1. Approved reference and simplified construction.
2. Pose, depth layers, and the central movement carrier with its visual handoffs.
3. Subject-related surrounding details and their placement.
4. Flat color relationships and irregular mark-making.
5. A short set of relevant exclusions.

For a photo-inspired request, use the short scene brief as the subject, not a
feature-by-feature transcription of the photo. The artwork controls construction;
the photo does not control likeness, exact placement, or anatomy.

Use the applicable prompt in the guide as a starting point, not a fixed script.
Avoid accumulating contradictory corrective instructions from rejected outputs.
For galleries, assign genuinely different axes and silhouettes rather than
requesting "varied angles" and accepting palette swaps. Preserve counts and
spacing, but do not use symmetry or repeated templates to tidy the drawing.
When the user wants new characters in the same accepted pose, keep that pose
fixed and vary the silhouette, feature relationships, and line emphasis.
Do not vary only hair and color. Describe relationships rather than demanding
the same geometric feature inventory for every face.

Keep the mapped source images and approved studies in their respective roles
across iterations. A new generation is not a replacement reference until the
user accepts it.

## Inspect and deliver

Inspect the actual generated result against the request and mapped references:

- Correct number of heads or people; no accidental duplicates or clipped heads.
- Requested eye count, with complete eye marks oriented to the head rather than
  the body; one visible eye per individual in the default single-eye treatment.
- Actual eye opening aligned to the head, not just its surrounding color patch;
  omit an optional second eye rather than preserving a misaligned addition.
- Unequal, irregular eye marks rather than identical stacked white diamonds;
  nose and mouth differ in weight and completeness rather than repeating icons.
- Flat, irregular construction rather than realistic portraits with grain.
- For photo-inspired scenes, the topic, subjects, and broad positions remain
  understandable, but photographic likeness, exact silhouettes, and camera
  geometry have not dictated the drawing. A faithful redraw with flat paint
  is a failure of this treatment, even if its colors and texture match.
- Small abrupt mouths, angular noses, and no animal-like muzzles.
- A fuller cheek and soft asymmetric chin taper in the head's own orientation,
  not identical eggs, triangular wedges, or needle points.
- In the sideways treatment, the whole head remains readable through its lower
  contour while a short local junction flows into the neck.
- Invented, non-anatomical head-neck relationships rather than believable rotated
  portraits; no generic repeated snout template.
- Meaningfully different requested positions without mechanically regularizing
  the features or correcting mixed viewpoints.
- Ear placement participates in the non-anatomical composition; a correctly
  positioned portrait ear must not quietly restore a conventional head structure.
- Hair roots follow the head's orientation while loose lengths fall with gravity;
  no upright scalp or hair originating from the neck. Female characters have
  long hair unless the user explicitly requests a different treatment.
- On sideways heads, no hair cap across the image-top-facing head edge; the
  hair flows downward rather than arching over that exposed contour.
- Broad calm color areas, varied black marks, and no invented lighting.
- A limited palette with unequal large fields and smaller repeated accents,
  rather than every swatch used equally or copied literally from a photograph.
- Figure-color continuity and intentional open ground; no automatic contrasting
  eye patches, split-color faces, or heavy dark background.
- For fusion, genuinely shared contours rather than two separated profiles.
- For symbolism, a discoverable relationship rather than an imposed icon.
- For complete scenes, meaningful setting, objects, and personal details remain
  legible and connected to the subject, not omitted or replaced by generic marks.
- Depth reads through overlap, scale, and cropping without shaded volume.
  In groups, combined contours and open gaps connect people into larger shapes;
  hair and gestures direct attention rather than merely decorating isolated figures.
- A dominant organizing element hands movement between forms at readable
  junctions; the route does not stop at each person's outline or rely only on
  repeated color. Shared faces produce an emergent shape rather than an overlay.
- Movement reads through contrasting leans, compressed and extended gestures,
  lifted steps, and responsive hair or clothing. Setting lines reinforce that
  action without competing with faces, hands, or meaningful contact.
- No unwanted hats, lettering, props, or extra bodies.
- If typography is requested, its wording, letterform treatment, scale, and
  placement are intentional; overlap does not obscure essential faces or gestures,
  and required text remains readable.

Separate objective checks from judgment: counting heads is not evidence that
the style is faithful. A user still judges resemblance and emotional effect.
If an output misses a requirement, identify the specific miss rather than
declaring success. Do not automatically retry failed, canceled, or timed-out
generation calls or run an unsolicited multi-image experiment.

Deliver the actual image or a working local file link with a short description
of what it explores. Do not claim exact replication or user approval of an
unreviewed output.

## Example requests

```text
/expressive-figurative-art Create ten hatless heads with varied positions, keeping the approved sheet's spare single-eye construction.
/expressive-figurative-art Paint a musician absorbed in rhythm, with a deeply sideways-bent head and simple shoulder gesture.
/expressive-figurative-art Create an original couple whose profiles morph through shared contours and subtly suggest a heart.
```
